newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OSCE urges Serbia to accept opposition victories.
newsitem.headline: OSCE urges Serbia to accept opposition victories.

text.p: Europe's security forum on Friday backed former Spanish premier Felipe Gonzalez's report on disputed November local polls in Serbia and called on Belgrade for prompt and full implementation of its recommendations.

Gonzalez concluded in his Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe report that the opposition fairly won polls in 13 key provincial centres and in the capital Belgrade and called on Serbian authorities to accept the result.

"The OSCE endorses the recommendations of Mr Gonzalez's report and calls for prompt and complete implementation," said Ambassador Lars Vissing of Denmark, whose country took over the chairmanship of the OSCE on January 1.

Vissing was speaking at a news conference after a special session of the OSCE's executive permanent council, called to discuss Gonzalez's report and a reply to it from Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic received earlier on Friday.

Milutinovic acknowledged that opposition parties had won a majority of votes in nine municipalities in Belgrade in the November 17 local elections but said Serbian authorities needed more detail to clarify results in others towns, including Serbia's second biggest city, Nis.

Serbian opposition parties rejected Milutinovic's reply as a smokescreen, effectively snubbing the OSCE recommendations and said their 46 days of protests over the annulment of their poll victories would go on.
Vissing said the 54-member OSCE wanted more time to study Milutinovic's letter, but it was clear the council's comments were made in the light of the foreign minister's reply.

The OSCE stressed that Gonzalez and his mission had in their hands the original protocols from the electoral commissions and had concluded that opposition parties had won in the disputed municipalities.
"It is not yet clear what Mr Milutinovic has based his findings on," Vissing said.

The letter was presented to the OSCE troika of Denmark, Switzerland and Poland -- representing current, past and future chairmen -- by Yugoslav deputy foreign minister Zivadin Jovanovic at a breakfast meeting on Friday.
Vissing said Jovanovic made no mention of whether Serbia's ruling Socialist Party was ready to hand over control of Belgrade to the opposition.
"What we are saying is "go back to the voting lists, give the seats on the municipal councils to those who were elected and not go for the idea of a re-election,'" Vissing said.
He said Denmark was ready to continue dialogue with Belgrade over improvements to the Serbian electoral system, in free media and an independent judiciary.
Jovanovic had apparently wanted to occupy Yugoslavia's seat on the permanent council during the special session, but this was rejected by other members.

Yugoslavia, comprising Serbia and Montenegro, was suspended in 1992 for its part in fuelling the war in neighbouring Bosnia. Vissing said Belgrade had to satisfy various conditions, apart from heeding the Gonazalez recommendations, before it would be accepted back into the body.

These include a return of OSCE missions to Yugoslavia, a resolution of the Kosovo problem -- the tense southern Serbian province where most of the population is Albanian -- and a settlement over the successor status of Yugoslavia.

Croatia and Bosnia want Belgrade to reapply to the OSCE as a new state and not as the successor to the former federation, a dispute which is bedevilling settlement of the debts and assets of the former Yugoslavia.
